title: Project management and the operating environment
apm_learning_objective: Understand project management and the operating environment.
exam_coverage_note: 6 of 60 marks. One exam question per learning outcome.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 1.1.1, 1.1.5 and 8th ed. 1.1, 1.1.4, 1.2, 1.3.2.

where_this_fits: This is the vocabulary objective. Six marks sit here, and the definitions you learn are reused all the way through the rest of the course. It is the cheapest objective in the syllabus to get completely right, so learn it first and learn it properly.

key_definitions.definition: A unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and achieve planned objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: A piece of work that hasn't been done in this exact form before, and that has a beginning and an end. When it's finished, it's finished.

key_definitions.definition: The ongoing, repeatable operational activity of an organisation, which sustains current performance rather than changing it.
key_definitions.plain_english: The work that keeps happening. Payroll runs every month, the helpdesk opens every morning. Nobody expects it to finish.

key_definitions.definition: The application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve specific project objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: Applying what you know, and how you work, to get a defined piece of change delivered.

key_definitions.definition: The coordinated management of related projects and business-as-usual activity to achieve outcomes and benefits that would not be available from managing them individually.
key_definitions.plain_english: Running several connected projects together because the whole is worth more than the parts.

key_definitions.definition: The selection, prioritisation and control of an organisation's projects and programmes so that they align with its strategic objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: Deciding which projects the organisation should be doing at all, and in what order.

key_definitions.definition: A technique for analysing the external environment across political, economic, sociological, technological, legal and environmental factors.
key_definitions.plain_english: A six-heading checklist for spotting what's going on outside the project that could land on it.

core_content.key_takeaway: A project is a unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and achieve planned objectives. Unique means this exact piece of work has not been done before in this form. Transient means it has a defined start and a defined end.
core_content.body_markdown:
Take the definition apart, because each part is doing a job.

Unique does not mean nobody has ever done anything like it. A housebuilder who has built two hundred houses is still running a project on the two hundred and first, because the site, the ground conditions, the buyer and the crew all differ. Unique means you cannot simply repeat what you did last time without thinking.

Transient means the team assembles, delivers, and disbands. This is the most reliable way to spot a project, because ongoing work can share almost every other characteristic.

To bring about change is the reason the project exists. It moves the organisation from one state to another. If nothing changes, no project was needed.

Achieve planned objectives tells you the change was intended and specified in advance. Change that happens by accident is not a project.

A useful test when something is described and you have to decide whether it is a project: ask when it finishes. If the honest answer is that it does not, it is ongoing work, whatever the description says about budgets or teams.

core_content.outcome_title: State the differences between a project and business as usual
core_content.key_takeaway: A project has a defined start and end, delivers change, produces a unique output, and uses a temporary team that disbands at the end. Business as usual is ongoing, sustains current operations, produces repeatable output, and sits with a permanent team. The clearest test is whether the work has a planned end.
core_content.body_markdown:
Organisations run both at the same time, and the difference decides how the work should be managed.

| Project | Business as usual |
|---|---|
| Defined start and end | Ongoing, no planned end |
| Delivers change | Sustains current operations |
| Unique output | Repeatable output |
| Temporary team, disbanded at the end | Permanent function |

You would not put a governance board and formal change control around the weekly payroll run, and you would not manage a brand new finance system as though it were a permanent service.

The relationship runs in one direction. Projects hand their outputs over to business as usual. A project builds the new payroll system, and business as usual then runs it every month.

core_content.key_takeaway: Project management is the application of processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve specific project objectives. It is a practice, not a piece of software, not governance, and not a job title.
core_content.body_markdown:
The definition says project management is an application of several things at once, and that matters because the exam offers answers that reduce it to only one of them.

It is not software. Scheduling tools support project management. They are not project management.

It is not governance. Governance sets the framework of authority the project works inside. Project management operates within that framework.

It is not a job title. A project can be managed well by someone whose title says something else, and holding the title does not mean the practice is being applied.

Keep the five ingredients in order: processes, methods, knowledge, skills, experience. The last two are the ones people forget. Someone following a flawless process with no judgement is not managing the project well, and the definition deliberately includes the human contribution.

core_content.outcome_title: State the key purpose of project management
core_content.key_takeaway: The purpose of project management is to achieve the project objectives within agreed constraints, and by doing so deliver beneficial change. Both halves count. A project delivered on time and on budget that leaves the organisation no better off has not achieved the purpose.
core_content.body_markdown:
There are two halves and they are tested separately.

The first half, objectives within agreed constraints, is the one everybody knows. Time, cost, quality and scope are agreed, and the project is managed to hold them.

The second half is the one that decides marks. The point of the work is beneficial change. A project run perfectly that leaves the organisation no better off has missed the purpose.

That leads to a distinction worth holding on to. A project delivers outputs: the new system, the finished building. Benefits are the measurable improvement that follows once someone uses those outputs. The project manager is accountable for the outputs. The sponsor is accountable for the benefits.

core_content.outcome_title: Define programme and portfolio management and their relationship with project management
core_content.key_takeaway: A programme coordinates related projects, alongside business as usual, to deliver benefits the projects could not deliver separately. A portfolio selects and prioritises an organisation's projects and programmes so that investment matches its strategy. Programme is coordination, portfolio is prioritisation.
core_content.body_markdown:
There are three levels and the exam tests whether you can separate them.

A project delivers a defined set of objectives. One set of outputs, one end.

A programme coordinates related projects, together with ongoing business activity, to deliver benefits that could not be achieved by running those projects separately. The key word is related. The parts are connected, and managing them together produces something extra.

A portfolio selects and prioritises the organisation's projects and programmes so that its investment matches its strategy. The contents do not need to be related at all. A portfolio might hold a building project, an IT migration and a marketing campaign side by side, and its job is to decide which of them should be funded, and in what order.

The relationship is a hierarchy but not a rigid one. Projects can sit inside programmes, and both sit inside portfolios. A project can also sit directly in a portfolio with no programme above it.

core_content.outcome_title: Describe why PESTLE analysis might be used by a project manager
core_content.key_takeaway: PESTLE is a structured scan of the environment outside the project: political, economic, sociological, technological, legal and environmental. A project manager uses it to identify external factors that could affect the project. It identifies those factors as an input to risk identification, and does not assess or prioritise them.
core_content.body_markdown:
PESTLE gives a project manager six fixed headings to scan the outside world against: political, economic, sociological, technological, legal and environmental.

It surfaces things the project does not control but will be affected by: a change of government, a movement in interest rates, a shift in public attitude, a new technology, a new regulation, a flood risk on the site.

The value is in the structure. Left to themselves, teams notice the categories they are already comfortable with, usually technological and economic, and miss the rest. Six fixed headings force attention onto the ones nobody in the room would raise.

What PESTLE produces is a list of factors to feed into risk identification. It tells you what is out there. It does not tell you how likely any of it is, how badly it would hurt, or what to do about it.

misconceptions.wrong: If it has a budget and a team, it's a project.
misconceptions.right: Business as usual has budgets and teams too. Transience and uniqueness are the only reliable discriminators, ask when the work finishes.

misconceptions.wrong: A programme is just a big project.
misconceptions.right: Size is irrelevant. A programme coordinates several related projects to produce benefits that managing them separately would not deliver. A very large single endeavour is still a project.

misconceptions.wrong: A portfolio is a collection of related projects.
misconceptions.right: That is a programme. A portfolio's contents need not be related at all, it is grouped by whose strategy the work serves, not by whether the work connects.

misconceptions.wrong: Project management guarantees the project will succeed.
misconceptions.right: It improves the odds and manages the constraints. Any exam option containing a guarantee is almost certainly a distractor.

misconceptions.wrong: Delivering the output on time and on budget means the project achieved its purpose.
misconceptions.right: The purpose is beneficial change. An output nobody adopts delivers no benefit, however well the delivery was managed.

misconceptions.wrong: PESTLE is a risk assessment technique.
misconceptions.right: It is an identification technique that feeds risk assessment. It produces no probability, no impact and no response.

misconceptions.wrong: Uniqueness means the project must be doing something never done before by anyone.
misconceptions.right: It means this particular endeavour, in this context, is not a straight repeat. The two hundredth house on a new site is still a project.

memory_aids.expansion: Political, Economic, Sociological, Technological, Legal, Environmental, the six external headings, and the only list in this objective you must recite.
Programme coordinates related projects. Portfolio prioritises against strategy. Two words, and the near-miss pair stops being a trap.
The one question that separates a project from business as usual. If the honest answer is 'it doesn't', it isn't a project.
The project delivers outputs. Benefits arrive when someone uses them. Project manager owns the first, sponsor owns the second.

progress_checkpoint: I can define a project and name the two words that do the work.
I can give three things a project and business as usual share, and the one thing that separates them.
I can define project management without mentioning software, governance or a job title.
I can state both halves of the purpose of project management, including beneficial change.
I can say which of programme and portfolio management is coordination and which is prioritisation.
I can expand PESTLE and explain why it identifies rather than prioritises.
